title: MATH GAOKAO - 16
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of an implication from the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the statement \(2+2=5\), and let \(q\) be the statement \(3+4=7\). What is the truth value of \(p\rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: The statement \(p\) is false because \(2+2=4\), not \(5\). The statement \(q\) is true because \(3+4=7\). An implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. Since \(p\) is false and \(q\) is true, the implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is true.
questions.hint: Recall that an implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a biconditional from the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the statement \(2>1\), and let \(q\) be the statement \(5\) is odd. What is the truth value of \(p\leftrightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: The statement \(p\) is true because \(2>1\). The statement \(q\) is true because \(5\) is odd. A biconditional \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have the same truth value. Since both are true, \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is true.
questions.hint: A biconditional is true when both components have the same truth value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a statement logically equivalent to a given implication.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to \(p\rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: For an implication \(p\rightarrow q\), the contrapositive is \(\neg q\rightarrow \neg p\), and it is logically equivalent to the original implication. The statement \(q\rightarrow p\) is the converse, which is not logically equivalent to \(p\rightarrow q\) in general.
questions.hint: Use the contrapositive, not the converse.

questions.learningObjective: Determine a statement equivalent to the negation of an implication.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to \(\neg(p\rightarrow q)\)?
questions.explanation:
An implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. Therefore, its negation is true exactly in that case, which is expressed by
\[
p\land \neg q.
\]
The statement \(\neg p\lor q\) is actually equivalent to \(p\rightarrow q\), not to its negation.
questions.hint: An implication fails only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a biconditional when the components have different truth values.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. What is the truth value of \(p\leftrightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: A biconditional \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have the same truth value. Here \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false, so they have different truth values. Therefore, \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is false.
questions.hint: Build a short truth table for the operations in the expression, then use the stated inputs to identify the relevant row.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the converse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: Which statement is the converse of “If \(x>2\), then \(x^2>4\)”?
questions.explanation:
For a conditional statement \(p\rightarrow q\), the converse is \(q\rightarrow p\). Here \(p\) is \(x>2\) and \(q\) is \(x^2>4\). Swapping them gives the converse:
\[
\text{If } x^2>4,\text{ then } x>2.
\]
Option B is the inverse, not the converse.
questions.hint: The converse swaps the hypothesis and the conclusion.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the inverse of a given conditional statement.
questions.question: Which statement is the inverse of \(p\rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation:
For a conditional statement \(p\rightarrow q\), the inverse is formed by negating both the hypothesis and the conclusion without swapping them:
\[
\neg p\rightarrow \neg q.
\]
Option B is the contrapositive, not the inverse.
questions.hint: The inverse negates both parts but does not swap them.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a biconditional when both components are true.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the statement \(3\) is prime, and let \(q\) be the statement \(4\) is even. What is the truth value of \(p\leftrightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: The statement \(p\) is true because \(3\) is prime. The statement \(q\) is true because \(4\) is even. Since both components are true, they have the same truth value. Therefore, the biconditional \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is true.
questions.hint: A biconditional is true when both components have the same truth value.

questions.concept: Equivalence of a Biconditional and Two Implications
questions.learningObjective: Identify a statement logically equivalent to a biconditional.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to \(p\leftrightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation:
The biconditional \(p\leftrightarrow q\) means that \(p\) implies \(q\) and \(q\) implies \(p\). Therefore,
\[
p\leftrightarrow q \equiv (p\rightarrow q)\land(q\rightarrow p).
\]
Option B only states one direction, so it is not equivalent to the biconditional.
questions.hint: A biconditional requires both directions of implication.

questions.learningObjective: Determine a statement equivalent to the negation of a biconditional.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to \(\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)\)?
questions.explanation:
The biconditional \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have the same truth value. Therefore, its negation is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have different truth values. This occurs when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false, or when \(p\) is false and \(q\) is true. Hence,
\[
\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)\equiv (p\land \neg q)\lor(\neg p\land q).
\]
Option B describes the cases where \(p\) and \(q\) have the same truth value, which is the original biconditional, not its negation.
questions.hint: Negate the condition “same truth value” to obtain “different truth values.”
